corpus_definition: To find something or meet someone by chance.
particle_note: Not separable: 'come across an old photo', never 'come an old photo across'. The object always goes after 'across'. Past: came across.

relations.note: Find is general; come across means you find it by chance, without looking for it.
Very close: to find something by chance, often something interesting.
Used for people: to meet someone you know by chance.
Informal, used for people: 'I bumped into my teacher at the bazaar.'
Related: to find something new or hidden, by chance or after searching.

context.text: While cleaning the cupboard, Malika came across her grandfather's old letters. Last week she also came across a classmate from school at Chorsu Bazaar.

reviewer_note: Only the 'find/meet by chance' sense; 'come across as' (seem) is a different meaning and is left out.

corpus_definition: to do something wrong or against the law.

forms.definition: the act of doing a crime or something wrong
forms.example: He was arrested during the commission of a robbery.
forms.note: Formal in this meaning. The everyday meanings of commission are money paid to a seller, or an official group.

syn.note: Very formal, used in legal English.

forms.definition: a promise to do something, or strong support for something
forms.example: Teaching every day needs a lot of commitment.
forms.note: Belongs to commit = promise or give yourself to something, not doing a crime.

forms.definition: to do something bad or against the law
forms.example: The police believe he committed the crime alone.
forms.note: Used with crime, murder, mistake, suicide, an offence.

syn.note: Neutral; can be used for good actions too, while commit is for bad ones.
Very formal, used in news and law.
Easy general word; commit shows the action is wrong.

forms.definition: working very hard for something you believe in
forms.example: She is a committed teacher who stays late to help students.
forms.note: Belongs to commit = give yourself to something, not doing a crime.
No common adverb in this family.

people.definition: a group of people chosen to make plans or decisions
people.example: The school committee meets every Monday.
people.note: Belongs to commit = give a job to someone (old meaning), not doing a crime. A committee is a group of people.

people.definition: an official in charge of a government department or group
people.example: The police commissioner spoke to journalists.
people.note: Goes with commission = an official group, not doing a crime.

context.text: The man who committed the robbery was caught the next day. In court, the judge described the commission of the crime in detail.

reviewer_note: Crime sense only; commitment/committed (promise, dedication), committee and commissioner marked other_meaning.

corpus_definition: The act of sharing thoughts or news with others.

forms.definition: the act of sharing ideas, news and feelings with other people
forms.example: Good communication is important in a team.
forms.note: The plural communications often means phones, radio and the internet.

syn.note: Contact means you talk or write to someone; communication is the whole sharing of ideas.
Interaction is any action between people, not only talking.
A conversation is one talk between people.

ant.note: When people do not understand each other correctly.

forms.definition: to share ideas, news or feelings with other people
forms.example: We communicate with our cousins in Moscow by video call.

syn.note: Easy word; talking is one way to share ideas.
To start contact with someone by phone, email or letter.
Formal: to make an idea or feeling known to others.

forms.definition: happy to talk and share information; connected with talking
forms.example: The new student is friendly and very communicative.

syn.note: Talkative means someone talks a lot; communicative means they share information well.
Easy word: happy to talk about your thoughts and feelings.

ant.note: Not willing to talk or give information.

forms.note: No common adverb; 'communicatively' is rare and used mostly about language teaching.

people.definition: a person who is good at sharing ideas with others
people.example: Our manager is a great communicator.

context.text: In our office, communication between teams is very important. We communicate every morning in a short meeting, and our boss is a clear communicator.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged into one map. Miscommunication and uncommunicative are listed as antonyms, not forms.

corpus_definition: Used to judge how two things are different or similar.

forms.definition: the act of looking at two things to see how they are different or similar
forms.example: The teacher made a comparison between city life and village life.

syn.note: A contrast looks only at the differences between things.
A careful study of something; a comparison is one kind.

forms.definition: the form of an adjective that shows more, like bigger or better
forms.example: The comparative of 'good' is 'better'.
forms.note: Belongs to grammar: the word form used with 'than', not a study that compares things.

forms.definition: to look at two things to see how they are different or similar
forms.example: Let's compare the prices in both shops before we buy.

syn.note: To show the differences between two things.
To think carefully about two choices before deciding.

forms.definition: studying how two or more things are different or similar
forms.example: She wrote a comparative study of schools in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.

syn.note: Used mostly in language study; looks especially at differences.
Careful: relative is close to comparative only in phrases like 'relative/comparative peace'.

forms.definition: similar in size, amount or quality to something else
forms.example: Prices in Tashkent are now comparable to prices in Almaty.
forms.note: Belongs to compare = be similar to, not a study that compares things.

forms.definition: more than usual when you think about other things; fairly
forms.example: The test was comparatively easy this year.
forms.note: Belongs to comparative = relative ('comparatively cheap'), not a study that compares things.

context.text: Our class did a comparative project on two cities. We had to compare Bukhara and Samarkand, and the comparison showed many similar old buildings.

reviewer_note: Comparative also names the grammar form (bigger, better); kept as other_meaning noun. Comparatively means 'relatively', so it is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: to give something to make up for a loss or problem

forms.definition: money or something else given to a person because of a loss or damage
forms.example: The airline paid us compensation for the lost suitcase.

syn.note: Any money you pay; compensation is paid because of a loss.
Legal word: money a court says someone must pay.
A refund gives back the money you paid; compensation can be more.

forms.definition: to give someone money or help because they lost something or were hurt
forms.example: The company agreed to compensate her for the damaged goods.
forms.note: Pattern: compensate someone for something; compensate for = make up for.

syn.note: Easy phrase: to return money you owe.
Easy phrasal verb: to do something good after something bad.
Formal: to pay back money someone spent.

forms.definition: given to a person to make up for a loss or damage
forms.example: The workers received a compensatory payment after the factory closed.

forms.note: No common adverb in this family.

context.text: When the bus company lost my bag, they agreed to compensate me. The compensation was enough to buy a new bag and new clothes.

reviewer_note: Compensatory is formal and rare for learners but real (Oxford, Cambridge); kept as an existing entry.

corpus_definition: To make something harder to understand or do.

forms.definition: something that makes a situation more difficult
forms.example: There was a complication with our visas, so the trip was late.
forms.note: In medicine it also means a new health problem during an illness.

syn.note: Easy general word; a complication is a problem that makes things harder.
Any hard situation or thing.
Informal: a small problem you did not expect.

forms.definition: to make something harder to understand or do
forms.example: Please don't complicate the plan with too many changes.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
To make something unclear, so people do not understand.

ant.note: To make something easier to understand or do.

forms.definition: having many parts, so it is hard to understand or do
forms.example: The rules of this game are very complicated.

syn.note: Very close; complex is a little more formal.
Easy word: hard to do or understand.
Hard to understand, not clear.

ant.note: Easy and clear, with no problems.

forms.note: No common adverb; 'complicatedly' is very rare.

context.text: Moving to a new flat was more complicated than we thought. Heavy rain complicated things, and there was another complication: the lift was broken.

reviewer_note: Complex is a synonym but not a family form; uncomplicated is listed as an antonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: Kind words said to someone to show you like something.

forms.definition: nice words you say to show you like or admire someone
forms.example: She gave me a nice compliment on my dress.
forms.note: Don't confuse with complement (something that goes well with another thing); same sound, different spelling.

syn.note: Praise is uncountable and often more serious; a compliment is one nice remark.
Nice words that are often not true, said to get something.

ant.note: Rude words that hurt someone's feelings.
Words saying what is bad about someone or something.

forms.definition: to say nice words to show you like or admire someone
forms.example: Everyone complimented Aziza on her plov.
forms.note: Pattern: compliment someone on something.

syn.note: Very close; praise is often used for work or actions.
To say nice things, often not true, to please someone.

ant.note: To say rude things to someone.
To say what is bad about someone. British spelling: criticise.

forms.definition: saying nice things that show you admire someone
forms.example: My teacher was very complimentary about my essay.
forms.note: Also means 'free', as in 'complimentary breakfast' at a hotel.

syn.note: Showing that you like and respect someone.
Saying nice things, sometimes more than is true.

ant.note: Saying what is bad about someone or something.

forms.note: No common adverb in this family.

context.text: At the wedding, guests complimented my aunt on the food. One compliment made her very happy, and everyone was complimentary about the music too.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: compliment (praise) vs complement (match well). The 'free' meaning of complimentary is in the note, not a separate entry.

corpus_definition: a person who writes musical pieces.

forms.definition: a person who writes music, especially for orchestras
forms.example: The composer wrote a lovely new symphony.

syn.note: A songwriter writes songs, usually pop music; a composer often writes longer pieces.
Anyone who plays or writes music.

forms.definition: a piece of music or writing that someone has created
forms.example: This composition was written for the piano.

syn.note: Easy word for one work of music: a piece by Mozart.
Anything created by an artist, writer or musician.

forms.definition: to write a piece of music
forms.example: He composed his first song when he was ten.

syn.note: Easy, general word; compose is used especially for music.
To make something new.

forms.definition: calm and in control of your feelings
forms.example: She stayed composed during the difficult exam.
forms.note: Belongs to compose = make yourself calm, not writing music.
No adverb for writing music; 'composedly' (calmly) is rare and belongs to the calm meaning.

context.text: Uzbek composers have written beautiful music for film and theatre. One famous composer composed a new piece for the Navruz concert in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); composition is an extra noun. Composed (calm) is other_meaning. Component shares an old Latin root but is not made from compose, so it is in people_not_family.

corpus_definition: a piece of writing or music created by someone.

forms.definition: a piece of music or writing that someone has created
forms.example: She finished her school composition last night.
forms.note: Also means what something is made of: 'the composition of the soil'.

syn.note: Easy word for one work of music or art.
A piece of writing for school; composition is a little old-fashioned in this meaning.
Anything created by an artist, writer or musician.

forms.definition: to write music, a poem or a letter
forms.example: She composed a short poem for her mother's birthday.

syn.note: Easy, general word; compose sounds careful and creative.
To make something new.

forms.definition: calm and in control of your feelings
forms.example: He looked composed before his speech.
forms.note: Belongs to compose = make yourself calm, not writing music or texts.
No adverb for writing music or texts.

people.definition: a person who writes music, especially for orchestras

context.text: For homework, Dilnoza composed a short song about spring. Her teacher liked the composition so much that she played it for the whole class.

reviewer_note: Kept the 'created work' sense; 'what something is made of' is only in a note. Composed (calm) is other_meaning. Component shares an old Latin root but is not made from compose, so it is in people_not_family.

forms.definition: a general idea or principle about what something is
forms.example: The basic concept is easy to understand.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with almost the same meaning.
A little formal; often an idea or belief that may not be right.
A basic rule or belief that explains how something works.
A set of ideas that tries to explain something.

forms.definition: an understanding of what something is or should be like
forms.example: Children have a different conception of time from adults.
forms.note: Also means the moment a woman becomes pregnant.

syn.note: Easy word: what you know about something.

forms.definition: to form an idea or plan in your mind
forms.example: He conceived the idea for the app while studying in Tashkent.
forms.note: Concept is made from this verb. It also means to become pregnant.

syn.note: Easy phrasal verb: to invent an idea or plan.
To make a picture of something in your mind.
Informal and common: to think of an idea.

forms.definition: to form a general idea of something in your mind
forms.example: It is hard to conceptualize how big the universe is.
forms.note: British spelling: conceptualise.

forms.definition: connected with ideas and principles, not real things
forms.example: The first part of the course is conceptual; the second part is practical.

syn.note: Based on ideas, not on practice.
About ideas, not about things you can see or touch.

ant.note: About real actions and use, not ideas.
Real and specific, something you can see or touch.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with ideas and principles
forms.example: Conceptually, the plan is simple, but it is hard to do.

syn.note: In theory, based on ideas, not on practice.

context.text: In our first lesson, the teacher explained the concept of saving money. The idea is conceptually simple, but many people find it hard to do.

reviewer_note: Concept comes from conceive, so conceive is listed as a family verb; its 'become pregnant' meaning is mentioned in the note.
